Theory of the Spinon-Mediated Witness Spin Glass in Herbertsmithite

Mitikorn Wood-Thanan Affiliation: School of Physics and Astronomy, Cardiff University, Cardiff CF24 3AA, United Kingdom Affiliation: School of Physics, University of Bristol, Bristol BS8 1TL, United Kingdom    Felix Flicker Affiliation: School of Physics, University of Bristol, Bristol BS8 1TL, United Kingdom
August 21, 2026
Abstract

Herbertsmithite is a prototypical candidate quantum spin liquid (QSL), believed to feature a long-range entangled ground state and deconfined fractionalised spinon excitations. Confirmation of these properties has been hindered by the presence of magnetic impurities (spin-1/2 Cu2+ spins substituted onto non-magnetic Zn2+ sites). Recently these impurities were reconceptualised as ‘witnesses’ of the QSL, inheriting long-range interactions and entanglement mediated by the QSL spinons, leading to spin glass formation amongst witnesses below 260260\,mK. Here we present a full theoretical account of this idea. Despite having only one free parameter (the witness-kagome spin coupling), our model captures the full range of experimental data, including: the formation of a spin glass amongst witnesses; the frequency and temperature dependence of the magnetic noise; a sharp peak in the DC magnetic susceptibility as a function of temperature; and the static neutron scattering structure factor at 22\,K. Both candidate QSLs (ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and U⁡(1)U(1)) give similar agreement with all data; however, our model predicts a qualitative difference between the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and U⁡(1)U(1) neutron scattering intensities below 260260\,mK, providing a long-sought definitive test to distinguish the two cases. We also predict phase diagrams as a function of temperature and witness concentration, finding a phase transition to different long-range ordered witness states for ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and U⁡(1)U(1) at high concentration.

I Introduction

Herbertsmithite (ZnCu3(OH)6Cl2) is a leading candidate to host a quantum spin liquid (QSL) Bert et al. 2007; Mendels and Bert 2010; Helton et al. 2010; Norman 2016; Broholm et al. 2020. This long-sought state of matter is characterised by the lack of magnetic order at absolute zero; long-range many-body entanglement; and deconfined fractionalised ‘spinon’ excitations Savary and Balents 2016; Balents 2010; Zhou et al. 2017; Broholm et al. 2020; Knolle and Moessner 2019; Wen 2002. A number of features of Herbertsmithite make it an excellent candidate to host this exotic quantum state of matter. In particular, it features quantum spin-1/21/2 Cu2+ ions on a kagome lattice with an antiferromagnetic (AFM) nearest neighbour exchange energy J≈−180J\approx-180\,K Shores et al. 2005; Helton et al. 2007; Misguich and Sindzingre 2007; Mendels and Bert 2010. These spins are expected to form a Kagome Heisenberg Antiferromagnet (KHAF), which numerical methods such as exact diagonalisation and DMRG predict to host either a U⁡(1)U(1) or ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL Ran et al. 2007; He et al. 2017; Yan et al. 2011; Lu et al. 2011; Depenbrock et al. 2012 (although more recent machine learning methods have brought this into question Durić et al. 2025). Evidence for the QSL in Herbertsmithite includes inelastic neutron scattering, which reveals a broad continuum of low-energy excitations consistent with spinons Helton et al. 2007; de Vries et al. 2009; Han et al. 2012a; Norman 2016.

However, definitive and unambiguous evidence of the QSL in Herbertsmithite remains lacking. A significant complicating factor is the presence of magnetic impurities. Hypothetically, the Cu2+ kagome planes are separated by triangular planes of non-magnetic Zn2+ ions, meaning the kagome layers are isolated 2D systems. In reality, 15-33% of the Zn2+ ions are substituted with spin-1/2 Cu2+ ions Lee et al. 2007; de Vries et al. 2008; Freedman et al. 2010. This could either mean that real Herbertsmithite crystals are non-stoichiometric (with an excess of Cu compared to the ideal composition), or that Zn ions substitute onto the Cu planes. These magnetic impurities are known to dominate the observed magnetic behaviour at low temperatures. For example, DC magnetic susceptibility below around 3030\,K is consistent with a signal coming entirely from impurities Bert et al. 2007, while inelastic neutron scattering at 22\,K shows broad features away from high-symmetry points which can be explained by AFM correlations, without long-range order, between nearest neighbour impurities Olariu et al. 2008; Han et al. 2016.

Recent experiments, to which the present authors provided theoretical support, identified previously unseen behaviour in Herbertsmithite at low temperatures Takahashi et al. 2026. Decreasing the temperature below T∗=260T^{*}=260\,mK, the DC magnetic susceptibility χ⁡(T)\chi(T) shows a sharp cusp. Below T∗T^{*} the noise spectrum of magnetization fluctuations as a function of frequency ff shows clear 1/f1/f behaviour (the noise magnitude rapidly disappears when heating above T∗T^{*}). Along with a lack of any indication of the onset of long-range magnetic order in earlier neutron scattering measurements at 22\,K, this behaviour pointed towards spin glass formation amongst impurities – recast as ‘witnesses’ in Ref. Takahashi et al. 2026 (nomenclature we adopt here). The spin glass behaviour was confirmed by observation of ageing phenomena: quenching from 400400\,mK to temperatures below T∗T^{*}, there is an excess of magnetic noise (above the 1/f1/f signal, and in violation of the fluctuation-dissipation theorem) at the lowest frequencies (corresponding to timescales of hours to days). This additional low-frequency noise power decays with time.

In this paper we present an expanded account of our theoretical model in Ref. Takahashi et al. 2026 that explained these observations. Taking inspiration from the proposal that spinons can mediate an RKKY interaction Legg and Braunecker 2019 (in which fermions mediate a long-range interaction between dilute magnetic impurities), we model the interactions between Cu2+ ‘witnesses’ as resulting from the QSL in the kagome layers. The basic picture is presented in Fig. 1: each witness, a copper ion sitting in a zinc layer, couples to the three copper ions in the kagome layers above and below. Each of these kagome copper ions couples to all other copper ions in the same kagome layer, owing to the long-range entanglement of the QSL. This leads to an indirect coupling between any pair of witness spins touching the same kagome layer.

We obtain the effective witness-witness interactions Ji​jJ_{ij} (where i,ji,j are witness sites) by integrating out the QSL using the kagome spin-spin susceptibility using a spinon-fermion mean field decomposition. To proceed, we use a simplified model in which the witness quantum spins-1/2 are reduced to classical Ising spins. This step is purely pragmatic, allowing us to use large-scale classical Monte Carlo methods to simulate witness correlations and dynamics. Despite the simplification, we find an excellent agreement with the full range of experimental results. We consider other possible models of witness interactions, including near-neighbour direct exchange and magnons; while some capture many of the results, none is compatible with all the observations.

We consider both candidate QSLs in Herbertsmithite: the gapped ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL, and the U⁡(1)U(1) QSL which has a Dirac Fermi surface. We find that both give qualitatively similar results. The ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL gives a quantitatively better match to the experimental data in every case, but the approximations in our model (such as classical witness spins and mean field QSL treatment) likely negate any meaningful difference.

Turning to new predictions, however, we find a qualitative difference between the behaviours of the candidate QSLs. While both QSLs give identical static neutron scattering patterns at 22\,K, with broad features as observed experimentally, we predict that below 260260\,mK (we look at 100100\,mK) the patterns are entirely different. New broad features develop in the U⁡(1)U(1) QSL compared to the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL. By clearly distinguishing between the candidate QSLs, such a measurement could provide the definitive evidence of the QSL itself.

We additionally make new predictions for the evolution of the spin glass as a function of witness concentration xx. Above a certain threshold of xx, the spin glass is replaced by a long-range ordered (LRO) phase. We find different long-range orders and correspondingly different threshold xx for U⁡(1)U(1) and ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}. While such concentrations cannot be reached physically, the forms of the hypothetical long-range order provide insight into the nature of the spin glass states at the natural concentration. In particular, we argue that the structure observed in neutron scattering Han et al. 2016 can be understood as (dynamically glassy) frustrated short-range ordered regions.

This paper proceeds as follows. In Sec. II we introduce our model of QSL-mediated interactions between witness spins. We outline certain basic assumptions and definitions in Sec. II.1. We detail the witness-witness interaction Hamiltonian in Sec. II.2 and the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and U⁡(1)U(1) QSL Hamiltonians in Sec. II.3. In Sec. II.4 we integrate out the QSLs to derive the effective witness-witness interactions Ji​jJ_{ij}. In Sec. III we detail our numerical Methods, specifically the large-scale classical Monte Carlo simulations of witness spins. In Sec. IV we present our results, showing a match to neutron scattering (Sec. IV.1), magnetic susceptibility (Sec. IV.2), the spin glass order parameter (Sec. IV.3), and the noise spectral density (Sec. IV.4). We make new predictions for the evolution of the behaviour with varying witness concentration in Sec. IV.5. In Sec. V we present our conclusions.

II Model

The basic assumption of our model is that witness interactions are mediated by the quantum spin liquid in the kagome layers. The picture to hold in mind is that of the RKKY interaction between magnetic impurities in the presence of a Fermi surface: clear evidence of a Fermi surface in Herbertsmithite would point towards the QSL, since the material is a band insulator. This story is complicated, however, by the fact that neither of the two candidate QSLs in Herbertsmithite has a spinon Fermi surface. The U​(1)​[0,π]U(1)[0,\pi] has pointlike Dirac nodes at the Fermi level Ran et al. 2007; Hermele et al. 2008, while the ℤ2​[0,π]​β\mathbb{Z}_{2}[0,\pi]\beta is gapped Lu et al. 2011. Nevertheless, an RKKY-type calculation can be performed, leading to different forms of interaction in the two cases.

II.1 Assumptions and definitions

We make the following assumptions on the nature of the impurities in Herbertsmithite.

  • •

    A proportion, xx, of Zn sites are occupied by magnetic Cu2+ ions with no corresponding defects in the kagome copper plane. Following the analysis in Ref. Takahashi et al. 2026, we set x=0.33x=0.33 unless otherwise mentioned.

  • •

    There is no back-action of the witnesses on the kagome copper spins.

  • •

    Witnesses do not induce any coupling between kagome planes.

We label witness sites (which live in Zn layers) i,ji,j and kagome sites (in Cu layers) l,ml,m.

II.2 Witness-Witness interactions

The idea of a spinon-mediated RKKY interaction was introduced in Ref. Legg and Braunecker 2019 and Ref. Dhochak et al. 2010. We treat the witnesses as dilute, and assume that each witness couples to the three kagome spins nearest to it in each of its two neighbouring kagome layers, via an interaction Hamiltonian

H^W​K=γ​s^W⋅s^K\displaystyle\hat{H}_{WK}=\gamma\hat{s}_{W}\cdot\hat{s}_{K} (1)

where s^W\hat{s}_{W} is the witness spin and s^K\hat{s}_{K} is the kagome spin. We assume that this coupling is incoherent: that is, we treat the coupling of the witness to each spin in the plaquette independently and neglect any coupling to the coherent superposition of the three spins together. This assumption is a conventional approach in the study of RKKY in graphene Saremi 2007; Black-Schaffer 2010; Power and Ferreira 2013.

Following the standard RKKY prescription, an interaction is induced between any pair of witnesses neighbouring the same kagome plane. Each witness couples to the three nearest kagome spins, and these kagome spins are coupled by the static spin susceptibility χl​m0\chi^{0}_{lm} of the QSL, where l,ml,m are kagome sites. The induced witness interaction is then

Ji​j=(γ2/4)∑l∈∴i∑m∈∴jχl​m0J_{ij}=(\gamma^{2}/4)\sum_{l\in\therefore_{i}}\sum_{m\in\therefore_{j}}\chi^{0}_{lm} (2)

where the sum is over the three kagome spins neighbouring witness spin ii (this triangle of spins being denoted ∴i\therefore_{i}). Witnesses then interact via

H^W​W=−∑i​jJi​js^i⋅s^j\displaystyle\hat{H}_{WW}=-\sum_{ij}J_{ij}\hat{s}_{i}\cdot\hat{s}_{j} (3)

where the sum is over all pairs of witnesses, and Ji​jJ_{ij} is non-zero whenever ii and jj neighbour the same kagome layer.

The static spin susceptibility can be calculated using

χl​m0=−1π∫−∞EFℑ𝔪[Gl​m(E)Gm​l(E)]dE\chi^{0}_{lm}=-\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{E_{F}}\mathfrak{Im}\left[G_{lm}\left(E\right)G_{ml}\left(E\right)\right]\text{d}E (4)

where EFE_{F} is the Fermi energy, and

Gl​m​(E)=⟨l|(E+i​η−H^QSL)−1|m⟩\displaystyle G_{lm}\left(E\right)=\langle l|\left(E+i\eta-\hat{H}_{\text{QSL}}\right)^{-1}|m\rangle (5)

is the real-space Green’s function connecting kagome sites ll and mm at energy EE (η\eta is a small positive regularisation) and H^QSL\hat{H}_{\text{QSL}} is the Hamiltonian describing the QSL.

We proceed to detail the forms of the two candidate QSL Hamiltonians in Herbertsmithite.

II.3 Candidate QSLs in Herbertsmithite

We make the standard assumption that the kagome layers in Herbertsmithite are well represented by the KHAF model

H^K​K=−J∑⟨l​m⟩s^Kl⋅s^Km\displaystyle\hat{H}_{KK}=-J\sum_{\langle lm\rangle}\hat{s}^{K}_{l}\cdot\hat{s}^{K}_{m} (6)

where J≈−180J\approx-180\,K Mendels and Bert 2010.

The Hamiltonian governing QSLs in the KHAF can be obtained by making a Schwinger fermion decomposition Ran et al. 2007

𝐬^lK=12​∑α​βf^l​α†​σα​β​f^l​β\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{s}}^{K}_{l}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha\beta}\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{l\alpha}{\mathbf{\sigma}}^{\alpha\beta}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l\beta} (7)

where f^l​α†\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{l\alpha} is a spinon creation operator on kagome site ll, α={↑,↓}\alpha=\{\uparrow,\downarrow\} labels the spin, and σ\mathbf{\sigma} is a vector of Pauli matrices. This decoupling unphysically doubles the size of the Hilbert space; physical states obey the constraint

∑αf^l​α†​f^l​α=1\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha}\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{l\alpha}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l\alpha}=1 (8)

on each site ii.

Under this substitution H^K​K\hat{H}_{KK} becomes quartic in spinon operators. Using a Hubbard Stratanovitch transformation this can be rewritten as a quadratic in spinon operators at the cost of introducing a new field ν^l​m\hat{\nu}_{lm} living on edges. Taking the mean field values of ν^l​m\hat{\nu}_{lm} then reduces the KHAF to a quadratic Hamiltonian in spinon operators:

H^K​K=−J∑⟨l​m⟩∑αν1t(1)l​mf^†l​αf^m​α+H.c.\displaystyle\hat{H}_{KK}=-J\sum_{\langle lm\rangle}\sum_{\alpha}\nu_{1}t^{(1)}_{lm}\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{l\alpha}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{m\alpha}+\textrm{H.c.} (9)

where the mean field value of ν^l​m\hat{\nu}_{lm} is ν1​tl​m(1)\nu_{1}t^{(1)}_{lm} with unit magnitude hoppings |tl​m(1)|=1|t^{(1)}_{lm}|=1.

Different QSLs can then be classified by the gauge flux passing through each triangle and hexagon in the kagome lattice (equivalently, by the Berry phase picked up by a spinon traversing one of these plaquettes). We proceed to list the two candidate mean field QSLs in Herbertsmithite.

II.3.1 U​(1)​[0,π]U(1)[0,\pi] QSL

The U​(1)​[0,π]U(1)[0,\pi] QSL has zero flux through triangles and π\pi flux through hexagons Hastings 2000; Ran et al. 2007; Hermele et al. 2008. It was previously found to have the lowest energy of all mean field U⁡(1)U(1) QSLs in the KHAF Ran et al. 2007. The required gauge fluxes can be achieved with real nearest neighbour spinon tight-binding hoppings tl​m(1)t^{(1)}_{lm} using a six-site unit cell (a doubling of the minimal structural unit cell, to accommodate the π\pi flux) as detailed in Ref. Ran et al. 2007. We use the same hoppings and unit cell definitions here, shown in Fig. 2. In these definitions all tl​m(1)t^{(1)}_{lm} have the same magnitude, and vary only in sign. The magnitude ν1\nu_{1}, which sets the overall spinon bandwidth, was reported in Ref. Hastings 2000 to be ν1=0.221\nu_{1}=0.221.

The resulting spinon bandstructure contains Dirac nodes at the Fermi level EFE_{F} He et al. 2017 (Fig. 3 and Fig. 4). Different gauge choices for the QSL (different hoppings leading to the same gauge fluxes) cause the Dirac nodes to move relative to the Brillouin zone, but the separation between the Dirac nodes is gauge invariant. This separation sets the RKKY wavevector.

II.3.2 ℤ2​[0,π]​β\mathbb{Z}_{2}[0,\pi]\beta QSL

The set of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} topologically ordered QSLs can be obtained from ‘parent’ U⁡(1)U(1) QSLs by introducing further-neighbour couplings so as to induce a mass gap Lu et al. 2011. Among the offspring of the U​(1)​[0,π]U(1)[0,\pi] QSL, only one, labelled ℤ2​[0,π]​β\mathbb{Z}_{2}[0,\pi]\beta, has a gap. For this reason it has also been proposed as a candidate QSL in Herbertsmithite.

Ref. Lu et al. 2011 sets up the following mean field spinon Hamiltonian:

λ3:1=∑l⟨f^l↑†​f^l↑⟩+⟨f^l↓†​f^l↓⟩.\lambda_{3}:\quad 1=\sum_{l}\left\langle\hat{f}_{l\uparrow}^{\dagger}\hat{f}_{l\uparrow}\right\rangle+\left\langle\hat{f}_{l\downarrow}^{\dagger}\hat{f}_{l\downarrow}\right\rangle. (21)

Following the standard self-consistent mean field method, we proceed to diagonalise the Hamiltonian

H^=∑l​m(γ^l​1†,γ^l​2†)​Dl​m​(γ^m​1γ^m​2)\hat{H}=\sum_{lm}\left(\hat{\gamma}_{l1}^{\dagger},\hat{\gamma}_{l2}^{\dagger}\right)D_{lm}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\hat{\gamma}_{m1}\\ \hat{\gamma}_{m2}\end{array}\right) (22)

with diagonal DD, and

{γ^l​α,γ^m​β}\displaystyle\left\{\hat{\gamma}_{l\alpha},\hat{\gamma}_{m\beta}\right\} ={γ^l​α†,γ^m​β†}=0\displaystyle=\left\{\hat{\gamma}_{l\alpha}^{\dagger},\hat{\gamma}_{m\beta}^{\dagger}\right\}=0 (31)

By inspecting the density of states we find a gap of 2​Δ=0.44​t12\Delta=0.44t_{1}. This is in good agreement with more exact methods. These are typically given in terms of JJ rather than t1t_{1}; the conversion is given as t1=0.4​Jt_{1}=0.4J by Ref. Ran et al. 2007 and t1=0.66​Jt_{1}=0.66J by Refs. Hastings 2000; Gregor and Motrunich 2008.

Previous estimates of the ℤ2​[0,π]​β\mathbb{Z}_{2}[0,\pi]\beta gap are 2​Δ/J=0.05±0.022\Delta/J=0.05\pm 0.02 Fu et al. 2015 (using nuclear magnetic resonance, which may be seeing either the singlet gap or triplet gap); 2​Δ/J=0.095±0.0252\Delta/J=0.095\pm 0.025 Yan et al. 2011 (Density Matrix Renormalisation Group (DMRG)); 2​Δ/J=0.172\Delta/J=0.17 Läuchli et al. 2019 (exact diagonalisation); and 2​Δ/J=0.132\Delta/J=0.13 Depenbrock et al. 2012 (DMRG). Our result compares remarkably well with the exact diagonalisation result of Ref. Läuchli et al. 2019, when using the conversion factor of Ref. Ran et al. 2007, which gives 2​Δ=0.43​t12\Delta=0.43t_{1}.

II.4 Witness-Witness Susceptibility Ji​jJ_{ij}

The witness-witness interaction Ji​jJ_{ij} is set by the kagome-kagome susceptibility as obtained in Sec. II.3. The expected form of interactions therefore depends sensitively on the type of QSL.

The standard RKKY interaction occurs between dilute magnetic impurities in the presence of a bulk Fermi surface. It takes the characteristic formKittlel 2004

Ji​jRKKY∝sin⁡(2​kF​ri​j)−2​kF​ri​j​cos⁡(2​kF​ri​j)ri​jD+1\displaystyle J_{ij}^{\textrm{RKKY}}\propto\frac{\sin(2k_F r_{ij})-2k_{F}r_{ij}\cos\left(2k_{F}r_{ij}\right)}{r_{ij}^{D+1}} (49)

where ri​jr_{ij} is the separation between impurities at positions ii and jj, and DD is the spatial dimension.

Importantly, however, neither of the candidate QSLs in Herbertsmithite has a bulk spinon Fermi surface. Therefore two other known results for RKKY-type interactions are relevant. The Fermi surface of Graphene takes the form of two Dirac nodes. Since graphene has D=2D=2 the general expression in Eq.49 would suggest a leading-order oscillatory 1/r21/r^{2} behaviour Kittlel 2004. In fact, the interaction takes the form

Ji​jgraphene∝1ri​j3.\displaystyle J_{ij}^{\textrm{graphene}}\propto\frac{1}{r_{ij}^{3}}. (50)

The fast decay comes from the Dirac nodal nature of the Fermi surface, while the lack of oscillations comes from the bipartite nature of the honeycomb lattice Saremi 2007. Importantly, the interaction is purely antiferromagnetic at all distances.

Bipartiteness means that the honeycomb lattice sites can be labelled A and B such that As only connect to Bs and vice versa. In Eq. (50) the impurities are assumed to lie at the centres of honeycomb hexagons. There are 6 honeycomb neighbours to each impurity, and so there are 36 honeycomb-honeycomb terms to sum over to get Ji​jJ_{ij}. Of these, half are AA or BB couplings and half are AB couplings. Combined with the relative strengths of AA/BB and AB, this results in the non-oscillatory pure AFM interactions of Eq. (50). We will find a similar, but less perfect, effect in the tripartite kagome lattice (Fig. 5).

The next relevant comparison is to gapped bilayer graphene. In this case the Dirac Fermi surface of graphene, with its associated Fermi velocity vFv_{F}, has disappeared with the introduction of a small energy gap of size Δ\Delta. The spin-spin susceptibility (no longer really an RKKY interaction) leads to a formParhizgar et al. 2013

Ji​jgapped graphene∝ri​j−3/2exp⁡(−2​Δ​ri​jℏ​vF).\displaystyle J_{ij}^{\textrm{gapped graphene}}\propto r_{ij}^{-3/2}\exp(-\frac{2\Delta r_{ij}}{\hbar v_F}). (51)

The interaction is again purely antiferromagnetic at all distances. While this is again a consequence of the bipartite lattice structure, we find a similar effect resulting from the tripartite structure of Herbertsmithite.

We proceed to calculate the static spin susceptibility for different QSLs using Eq. (4). We carry out the energy integral numerically. We obtain the real-space Green’s functions as a function of energy using exact diagonalisation of finite size clusters in real space; as a check, we also perform an analytic Fourier transform and redo the calculation in kk-space. The results are identical up to real-space boundary effects.

II.4.1 U⁡(1)U(1) QSL

Working in real space we carry out exact diagonalisation of a 32×3232\times 32 unit cell cluster (with 6 kagome sites per cell). We used 2×1052\times 10^{5} steps in the numerical energy integral, with the regularisation η=10−3\eta=10^{-3}\,meV in Eq.(5). The resulting Ji​jJ_{ij} is shown in Fig. 6. The interactions are purely antiferromagnetic everywhere; we find the interaction decays with distance as Ji​j∝r−3J_{ij}\propto r^{-3}.

At first sight the excellent agreement is surprising: while both 2D, the graphene and Herbertsmithite lattices are different. In particular, Herbertsmithite is not bipartite, although it is tripartite, meaning it has three sublattices A, B, C such that A only connects to B and C, and so on.

On closer inspection, though, the arguments presented for graphene in Ref. Saremi 2007 carry over well to Herbertsmithite. The key observation is that, while the standard RKKY interaction is a function of kF​ri​jk_{F}r_{ij}, with a pointlike Dirac Fermi surface there is no notion of Fermi wavevector kFk_{F}. The relevant inverse lengthscale is instead set by 𝐤D\mathbf{k}_{D}, the wavevector separating inequivalent Dirac nodes. The Dirac nodes must lie at high symmetry points in the Brillouin zone. As a result, cos⁡(2​𝐤D⋅𝐫i​j)\cos(2\mathbf{k}_D\cdot\mathbf{r}_{ij}) takes special values (integer/half-integer) on all lattice sites. It is this that leads to the complete disappearance of any oscillatory terms in Eq. (50).

Essentially the same arguments work for the U⁡(1)U(1) QSL in Herbertsmithite. Here the locations of Dirac nodes in the Brillouin zone are gauge dependent, but the separation between inequivalent nodes, 2​𝐤D2\mathbf{k}_{D}, is a gauge invariant quantity Ran et al. 2007. Just as in graphene, cos⁡(2​𝐤D⋅𝐫i​j)\cos(2\mathbf{k}_D\cdot\mathbf{r}_{ij}) takes on special integer/half-integer values on all lattice sites. With witnesses sat a above/below the centres of triangles, there are 9 kagome-kagome susceptibilities to sum over in Eq. (2) (see Fig. 5). There are one each of AA, BB, CC, couplings, which we find to be ferromagnetic and weak; then there are a total of six AB, BC, AC couplings which we find to be of equal strength to one another, stronger than the AA type couplings, and antiferromagnetic. Overall, the effect, as in graphene, is to produce a non-oscillatory purely AFM witness-witness interaction. Combined with the random witness site occupation, this frustrating long-range AFM interaction leads to spin glass behaviour.

II.4.2 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL

Working in real space we carry out exact diagonalisation of a 16×1616\times 16 unit cell cluster. The reduced number compared to the U⁡(1)U(1) case is a result of the matrix structure of the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Hamiltonian.

The resulting Ji​jJ_{ij} is shown in Fig. 7. The interactions are almost purely antiferromagnetic as before. The results compare well to the analytic form for gapped graphene, Eq. (51), with Δ/vF\Delta/v_{F} the result of our self-consistent calculation. Some Ji​jJ_{ij} in our calculation are ferromagnetic (but smaller than the corresponding antiferromagnet interactions at similar distances). These reduced-strength sites seem not to be numerical artefacts, as they appear for different system sizes and numerical regularisations. They also match the lattice symmetries despite the system boundaries not doing so. Broadly, though, the gapped graphene analytical function remains a decent rule of thumb for the Ji​jJ_{ij} in the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL. We nevertheless use the results of our numerical calculations in the subsequent sections.

II.4.3 Magnons

Early theoretical studies on the KHAF calculated a spin-spin susceptibility using the Kondo-Yamaji Green’s function method Bernhard et al. 2002; Legg and Braunecker 2019. These calculations are interesting for two reasons. First, the susceptibility can be attributed to magnons despite the lack of long-range magnetic order. Second, the calculation remains agnostic to the particular form of QSL ansatz, focussing instead on the microscopic spin interactions.

Reproducing this calculation, we converted the result to real-space Ji​jJ_{ij} terms using a Fourier transform. The result is shown in Fig. 8. We find that the interactions decay as 1/r21/r^{2} in most directions, but decay as 1/r1/r along certain high symmetry directions. These slow decays lead to divergent sums over spin interactions: the spins along a circle of radius RR around a given point contribute more for larger RR. As well as being unphysical (the energy of such a set of interactions would diverge), this leads to an incorrect prediction for neutron scattering. This rules out a magnon-mediated witness interaction of this form as a possible explanation for the observations in Herbertsmithite.

III Monte Carlo Methods

Having identified the couplings Ji​jJ_{ij} between witnesses in Sec. II, we proceed to simulate their dynamical and equilibrium behaviours. In order to simulate sufficiently large system sizes and run times to capture spin glass behaviour, from here on we approximate the witnesses to be classical Ising spins (nominally aligned along cc). We then create a classical Monte Carlo simulation of the witness spins using the Metropolis-Hasting algorithm Newman and Barkema 2001.

The physical space represented by the simulation is a rhombic prism with the x​yxy-planes forming the rhombic cross-section, as illustrated by Fig. 9. We indicate the size of the simulated lattice using the following notation: X×Y×ZX\times Y\times Z with Y=XY=X. Note that this space has a different orientation to the usual crystallographic Herbertsmithite unit cell as defined in Ref. Braithwaite et al. 2004. In this notation, XX indicates the side length of the rhombic cross-section equal to the number of witnesses and each integer ZZ corresponds to a single period of the ABC stacking (i.e. three layers of the witness plane). The side length and height of the rhombic prism are, respectively, X​a3X\frac{a}{\sqrt{3}} and Z​cZc, where a=6.834a=6.834\,Å and c=14.075c=14.075\,Å are Herbertsmithite’s unit cell parameters Braithwaite et al. 2004. We further take the simulated lattice to have periodic boundary condition in all directions. As each ZZ layer contains three witness planes, we require that XX is a multiple of three. Furthermore, although not a strict requirement, we only simulate lattices with even ZZ. As the models we are simulating include predominantly AFM interactions between nearest witness planes, we expect that a simulated lattice with odd ZZ and periodic boundary condition could exhibit artificial frustration along the zz-axis. For the results reported in this paper, we use X=45X=45 and Z=4Z=4 for our simulated lattice. An exception to this is when the spins exhibit long-range ordering, where we use X=48X=48 in order to avoid suppressing the ordering.

To start a simulation run, we randomly assign Nw=x​X2​ZN_{w}=xX^{2}Z of the sites to be occupied by Cu2+ witnesses. The location of the witnesses is assigned using a seeded random number generator to allow us to isolate behaviours that are the result of a specific witness configuration versus a general behaviour of the model. All runs where x<1x<1 are performed on 128 different seeds that are kept identical between runs.

To thermalise and simulate the system at thermal equilibrium, we update it through a Monte Carlo (MC) sweep. A single MC sweep involves NwN_{w} spin flip attempts, where each spin flip attempt involves picking a random witness and reversing the spin (1→−11\rightarrow-1 and vice versa). To ensure that detailed balance holds, each spin flip attempt has max(e−ΔE/kBT,1)\text{max}(e^{-\Delta E/k_{B}T},1) chance of being accepted, where Δ​E\Delta E is the change in energy due to the spin flip.

Once the configuration of witness sites has been specified, we initialise the system with randomly oriented spins. We then run our simulation starting at an initial temperature Ti≫T∗T_{i}\gg T^{*} and ending at final temperature TfT_{f} using steps of Ts​t​e​pT_{step}. At each temperature, the system is first equilibrated through Ne​qN_{eq} MC sweeps. Following equilibration, we then perform NTN_{T} MC sweeps to obtain our samples for calculating physical observables. For our results, we used Ne​q=N_{eq}= 2,000 MC sweeps and NT=N_{T}= 100,000 MC sweeps.

Here, the thermal averaging ⟨⋯⟩\langle\cdots\rangle indicates an average of the corresponding quantity over all MC sweeps performed at thermal equilibrium. Implicitly, all reported observables are additionally averaged over disorder—being the 128 different seeded witness configurations—at the final step.

We begin with the DC susceptibility χ⁡(T)\chi(T) (not to be confused either with the static spin susceptibility χ0\chi^{0} or with the spinon hopping parameters χl​m\chi_{lm}), which we calculate from the fluctuations of the magnetization. We define the magnetization here as magnetization per spin,

m=1Nw​∑i=1Nwsi,\displaystyle m=\frac{1}{N_{w}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{w}}s_{i}, (52)

where si=±1s_{i}=\pm 1 for Ising spins. The DC susceptibility (per spin) is obtained as the variance of the magnetization,

χ=NwT​(⟨m2⟩−⟨m⟩2).\displaystyle\chi=\frac{N_{w}}{T}\left(\langle m^{2}\rangle-\langle m\rangle^{2}\right). (53)

We use the location of the cusp in χ\chi to identify the glass transition temperature T∗T^{*}.

We use the Edwards-Anderson order parameter qEAq_{\textrm{EA}} to characterise spin freezing. This quantity measures whether the spins in the configuration, on average, remain in the same orientation over time. It is defined as

qEA=1Nw​∑i=1Nw⟨si⟩2.\displaystyle q_{\textrm{EA}}=\frac{1}{N_{w}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{w}}\langle s_{i}\rangle^{2}. (54)

A shortcoming of the Edwards-Anderson order parameter is that it also goes to unity for any phase where the spins become static, such as an AFM phase, and not just spin glass. In the case of spin glass, we expect that conventional real-space order parameters, such as the absolute magnetization ⟨|m|⟩\langle|m|\rangle and the AFM order parameter ⟨qAFM⟩\langle q_{\textrm{AFM}}\rangle, would remain nearly zero as per the paramagnetic phase. We defined qAFMq_{\textrm{AFM}} as

qAFM=1Nw​|∑i=1Nw(−1)α​si|,\displaystyle q_{\textrm{AFM}}=\frac{1}{N_{w}}\left|\sum_{i=1}^{N_{w}}(-1)^{\alpha}s_{i}\right|, (55)

where α=±1\alpha=\pm 1 is the sublattice index; i.e. its sign alternates between x​yxy-planes in real space.

We calculate the energy-integrated neutron scattering intensity S⁡(𝐪)S(\mathbf{q}) using

S⁡(𝐪)=|F⁡(𝐪)|2​⟨|∑isi​exp⁡(i​𝐪⋅𝐫i)|2⟩\displaystyle S(\mathbf{q})=\left|F(\mathbf{q})\right|^{2}\left\langle\left|\sum_{i}s_{i}\exp\left(i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{i}\right)\right|^{2}\right\rangle (56)

and the noise spectral density as

S⁡(f)=|∑tNT∑iNwsi​(t)​exp⁡(2​π​i​f​t)|2.\displaystyle S(f)=\left|\sum^{N_{T}}_{t}\sum^{N_{w}}_{i}s_{i}(t)\exp\left(2\pi ift\right)\right|^{2}. (57)

Here NTN_{T} is the number of sampling MC sweep in the simulation and F⁡(𝐪)F(\mathbf{q}) is the Cu2+ atomic form factor Han et al. 2016, which we use in our plots. As we do not have a physical timescale with which to convert Monte Carlo time steps into physical time units, the frequency ff is in arbitrary units.

IV Results

IV.1 Neutron Structure Factor

In Fig. 10, we plot our predicted static/energy-integrated neutron scattering intensity S⁡(𝐪)S(\mathbf{q}) at T=2T=2\,K. The results can be compared directly with the experimental and theoretical results in Fig. 1 of Ref. Han et al. 2016. We use the same form factor as indicated in that work. As noted in that paper, the key features are a diffuse ring of scattering in the HK0 plane, and broad peaks (not diffraction limited) in the HHL plane at 00⁤3200\frac{3}{2} and 12​12​0\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{2}0. Both the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and U⁡(1)U(1) QSLs reproduce these features well. Ref. Han et al. 2016 shows that the HHL peaks can be reproduced by a simple model of AFM correlations, without long-range order, between nearest neighbour witnesses (which are displaced along cc).

The experimental HHL scattering pattern, in particular, places a strong constraint on possible interactions between witnesses. It suggests that (i) the nearest neighbour witness-witness interactions should be antiferromagnetic; (ii) further neighbour interactions must exist to frustrate the formation of long-range order; (iii) the strengths of further neighbour interactions must decay sufficiently quickly with distance that other features do not appear. The necessity of (ii) is clear from the fact that the nearest neighbour structure alone has the connectivity of the simple cubic lattice; it is therefore bipartite and unfrustrated with AFM interactions.

The necessity of (iii) is demonstrated clearly by the non-QSL model of Sec. II.4.3, in which witness interactions are mediated by magnons. In this case the couplings Ji​jJ_{ij} are found to obey criteria (i) and (ii), but the AFM couplings decay with distance rr as 1/r21/r^{2}, or even 1/r1/r along high symmetry directions. As a result, sums over spins are divergent: the sum of contribution of spins at radius RR grows with RR. One effect of this is that the neutron scattering pattern cannot match experimental observations, and such a model can be neglected.

The neutron scattering data therefore constrain possible models of witness interactions as follows: interactions must be antiferromagnetic at nearest neighbour; frustrated by further neighbour interactions; and must decay at least as fast as 1/r21/r^{2} (which is in any case a physical requirement for quasi-2D systems). Fig. 10 shows that both QSL candidates in Herbertsmithite meet these criteria. Unfortunately, they lead to essentially indistinguishable scattering patterns at 22\,K, meaning the existing neutron data cannot discern between the two possibilities.

However, turning our attention to possible near term experiments, in Fig. 11 we show the predicted neutron scattering patterns at 100100\,mK, within the spin glass regime for both models. In both QSLs, the 00⁤3200\frac{3}{2} feature has sharpened and in so doing has moved towards 15​15​32\frac{1}{5}\frac{1}{5}\frac{3}{2}. We further observe a qualitative difference between the two candidate QSLs. The ratio S⁡(12​12​0)/S⁡(15​15​32)S(\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{2}0)/S(\frac{1}{5}\frac{1}{5}\frac{3}{2}), which was around 1 at 22\,K, has decreased to around zero for the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL, but for the U⁡(1)U(1) QSL it has actually increased to greater than one. A new feature has also appeared in the U⁡(1)U(1) pattern at 12​12​3\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{2}3 which again outweighs the 15​15​32\frac{1}{5}\frac{1}{5}\frac{3}{2} peak; this feature is absent in the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} pattern. These clear differences between the neutron scattering predictions for the two QSLs at low temperatures offer a route to definitively identifying which is present in Herbertsmithite.

It can be helpful to imagine starting from the long-range order observed in the x=1x=1 case (see Sec. IV.5) and randomly removing sites. The neutron scattering at the physical concentration can then be thought of as residual ordering in local witness clusters. For instance, the diffuse peak for U⁡(1)U(1) at 12​12​0\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{2}0 and 12​12​3\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{2}3, corresponds to nearest neighbour ferromagnetic correlation. Although this may appear counterintuitive as all couplings for the U⁡(1)U(1) model are antiferromagnetic, the same correlation can also be observed in the long-range order phase for U⁡(1)U(1) in Sec. IV.5. This suggests that the spin glass in our model can be thought of as glassy short-range ordered regions where each region exhibits similar correlation to the long-range order phase.

IV.2 DC Magnetic Susceptibility

In Fig. 12 we reproduce the measured DC magnetic susceptibility data χ⁡(T)\chi(T) from Ref. Takahashi et al. 2026, showing the cusp at T∗=260T^{*}=260\,mK. We also show our predictions based on both ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and U⁡(1)U(1) QSLs. In both cases we have constrained the one free parameter in our model, the witness-kagome coupling γ\gamma, to give a match to the observed Curie-Weiss temperature of TCW=1.1T_{\textrm{CW}}=1.1\,K. Experimentally, TCWT_{\textrm{CW}} is found by a linear fit to χ​(T)−1\chi(T)^{-1} at high temperature extrapolated to find the negative of the x−x-intercept. As a result, constraining to the Curie-Weiss temperature causes our models to agree with the experimentally observed χ⁡(T)\chi(T) at high temperatures. We note that constraining γ\gamma does not affect the ratio TCW/T∗T_{\textrm{CW}}/T^{*}.

We find that the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL gives T∗=0.15T^{*}=0.15\,mK while the U⁡(1)U(1) QSL gives T∗=0.11T^{*}=0.11\,K. In both cases T∗T^{*} is heavily suppressed compared to TCW=1.1T_{\textrm{CW}}=1.1\,K, as in the experiment. This is a measure of the frustrating effect of further-neighbour interactions. The higher value of T∗T^{*} in the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL compared to U⁡(1)U(1) can similarly be understood as relatively less frustration, since Ji​jJ_{ij} decay exponentially for ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and only algebraically, as 1/r31/r^{3}, for U⁡(1)U(1). The ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} prediction is closer to the experimental value, but the approximations in our model (notably the classical Ising nature of the witnesses, and the use of mean field theory in the QSL calculations) likely negate the possibility of drawing any inferences from these small differences.

We also show in Fig. 13 the result of a model that includes only nearest and next nearest neighbour witness interactions. The divergence at low TT is representative of the behaviour of any such local interaction models. It can be understood as follows. Even though the majority of witnesses form a single large connected cluster with second-nearest neighbour interactions and x=33x=33% site occupation, a significant minority of witnesses are isolated or are member of small clusters whose interaction is dominated by frustration from the next nearest neighbour coupling. These behave paramagnetically, giving a divergent susceptibility at low TT that ultimately dominates the signal. Any models based only on near neighbour witness exchange will fail to form a connected cluster across the bulk, adding another constraint on possible models. For this reason, even if appropriate witness exchange pathways could be identified in Herbertsmithite, an explanation of the experimental data would be unlikely to succeed even with significant fine tuning.

It is notable that, even though the interactions induced by the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL decay exponentially with a decay range of less than one lattice site, the exponential tail of this interaction nevertheless succeeds in connecting all witnesses into a single connected component, thus avoiding a divergent χ⁡(T)\chi(T) at low temperatures.

IV.3 Spin Glass Order Parameter

In Fig. 14 we show the Edwards-Anderson spin glass order parameter qEAq_{\textrm{EA}}. We show the experimental values of qEAq_{\textrm{EA}} from Ref. Takahashi et al. 2026, which were obtained in that paper using

χ⁡(T)∝1−qEA​(T)T−TCW​(1−qEA​(T)).\displaystyle\chi(T)\propto\frac{1-q_{\textrm{EA}}(T)}{T-T_{\textrm{CW}}\left(1-q_{\textrm{EA}}(T)\right)}. (58)

The experimental data show qEAq_{\textrm{EA}} turning on smoothly below T∗T^{*}, the temperature of the cusp in χ⁡(T)\chi(T). Our QSL predictions mirror this behaviour, with the respective T∗T^{*} seen in the models. Additionally, we observe ⟨qAFM⟩=0\langle q_{\textrm{AFM}}\rangle=0 in our models, ruling out the possibility of long-range AFM order. The neutron scattering is not featureless, however, suggesting that the spin glass possesses localised AFM correlated regions. We return to this in Section IV.5.

IV.4 Noise Spectral Density

In Fig. 15 we show the magnetization noise spectral density S⁡(f,T)S(f,T) as a function of frequency ff. Again matching the experimental data of Ref. Takahashi et al. 2026, we find white noise (SS independent of frequency) for T>T∗T>T^{*} which turns over to S∝1/fS\propto 1/f ‘pink’ noise below T∗T^{*}. This is a well-documented behaviour of spin glasses Ocio et al. 1985; Weissman 1993; Atalaya et al. 2014.

IV.5 Varying Witness Concentration

Our model suggests that the magnetic impurities in Herbertsmithite can act as a direct probe of the properties of the QSL Takahashi et al. 2026. While earlier studies were motivated to reduce the concentration of impurities, seeing them as an obstacle to observing the QSL, this new perspective begs the question as to how differing impurity concentration xx can affect the properties of Herbertsmithite.

Reported impurity concentrations for Herbertsmithite vary substantially between analyses and samples. A recent study reported 11% Zn-in-kagome, but with nearly stoichiometric Zn:CuKremer et al. 2025. Earlier work reported a synthesis that resulted in stoichiometric Herbertsmithite with 7% antisite disorder as well as another sample that is Cu-deficient, with 11% of Cu site occupied by Zn ions de Vries et al. 2012. Another study reported 15% of Zn site occupied by Cu with no significant Zn occupation in Cu sites Freedman et al. 2010. In our model, this corresponds to a witness occupation of x=0.15x=0.15. However, Ref. Takahashi et al. 2026 revisited earlier X-ray diffraction data taken on the same crystals Kremer et al. 2025, and, based on the Curie-Weiss fitting, calculated the witness occupation to be x=0.33x=0.33. Several experimental studies have reported that Zn substitution into Cu planes is unlikely Freedman et al. 2010; Han et al. 2012b, and on that basis it has been claimed that there is a minimum possible value of xx (then reported as x=0.15x=0.15). In the opposite limit, it is known that a structural phase transition occurs at around x=0.66x=0.66 where the crystal loses its undistorted kagome lattice structure Norman 2016. Given these constraints, we expect that our theoretical model is only applicable to Herbertsmithite with impurity concentration between 0.15<x<0.660.15<x<0.66. However, owing to finite system sizes in our simulation, the precise values of xx we report are likely inaccurate, although we would expect that the broad trends would match what would be seen. To better understand the behaviour of our model, we thus conducted numerical calculations for 0≤x≤10\leq x\leq 1.

In Fig. 16 we show the evolution of the DC magnetic susceptibility χ⁡(T)\chi(T) and specific heat C⁡(T)C(T) with varying xx for both QSLs. As xx increases, the cusp in χ⁡(T)\chi(T) moves to higher temperatures: higher witness concentration means higher witness density and therefore overall stronger interactions. We further observe that, at high xx, the specific heat develops a sharp step. This is indicative of a phase transition to long-range ordering rather than spin glass. This fits the intuition that the lack of disorder at x=1x=1 means that we expect some form of ordered state at low temperature rather than spin glass.

We carried out numerical simulations for 0≤x≤10\leq x\leq 1 at intervals of x=0.05x=0.05. These results indicate that a first-order phase transition occurs at sufficiently large x≈0.95x\approx 0.95 for ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and x≈0.75x\approx 0.75 for U⁡(1)U(1). At these concentrations, enough witnesses exist to make long-range ordering energetically favourable. The LRO pattern differs between the two QSLs; their ordering is illustrated in Fig. 17. In both cases, the LRO phase shows a striped pattern in the x​yxy-plane with 3-fold degeneracy up to translational and spin inversion symmetry. This result is consistent with previous studies of AFM models on the triangular lattice (recalling that witnesses occupy a triangular lattice between kagome layers) where long-range interactions result in stripe orderKorshunov 2005. In particular, Ref. Koziol et al. 2023 demonstrates that AFM coupling with power law decay generally exhibits stripe ordering on the triangular lattice. This is consistent with the ordering pattern of U⁡(1)U(1) QSL model on the same witness plane.

Using these data, in Fig. 18 we construct phase diagrams for both the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and U⁡(1)U(1) QSLs as a function of xx and TT. At low witness concentration x<0.15x<0.15, we find the paramagnetic phase freezing to spin glass as indicated by qEAq_{\textrm{EA}} approaching unity as T→0T\rightarrow 0. However, we are not able to report the precise T∗T^{*} due to a lack of cusp in χ⁡(T)\chi(T). At x>0.15x>0.15, we identify a clear spin glass transition temperature T∗T^{*}. The quantity reported in this diagram shows the average with respect to site disorder with a standard deviation of 2020\,mK.

Though the phase diagrams for both QSLs are qualitatively similar, we can see the effect of the interaction range on the phase diagram. We can see that the LRO phase is more vulnerable to missing-site disorder for the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL’s exponentially decaying Ji​jJ_{ij}, compared to the U⁡(1)U(1) QSL’s algebraic 1/r31/r^{3} decay. Short-range interactions mean that local ordering of sites is much more vulnerable to being disrupted by missing sites. Our models predict that the threshold between spin glass and LRO phase sits outside of the physically meaningful range for Herbertsmithite. However, if this transition were observed in higher impurity samples, it would be indicative of long-range coupling between witnesses.

V Conclusions

We have detailed our model, presented in part in Ref. Takahashi et al. 2026, of spin glass formation amongst spin-1/2 Cu2+ impurities (‘witnesses’) on Zn2+ sites in Herbertsmithite as originating from interactions mediated by the quantum spin liquid (QSL) in the kagome copper layers. Our model has only one free parameter: the strength of witness-kagome coupling γ\gamma which we constrain to γ=±60\gamma=\pm 60\,K by requiring a Curie-Weiss temperature of TCW=1.1T_{\textrm{CW}}=1.1\,K. Despite this, we find a good quantitative and qualitative match to the full range of existing experimental data, including: a cusp in the DC magnetic susceptibility χ⁡(T)\chi(T) at a temperature T∗T^{*} well below TCWT_{\textrm{CW}}; the smooth turning on of an Edwards-Anderson order parameter qEAq_{\textrm{EA}} at T∗T^{*}; the full frequency and temperature dependence of the noise spectral density S⁡(f,T)S(f,T); and the elastic neutron scattering intensity S⁡(𝐪)S(\mathbf{q}) in both the HK0 and HHL planes at 22\,K. We have additionally made new predictions for future experiments, including a phase diagram for the predicted behaviour as a function of witness concentration xx. Importantly, we find that if elastic neutron scattering can be undertaken below 260260\,mK, the two candidate QSLs, ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and U⁡(1)U(1), can readily be distinguished owing to the appearance of a strong broad peak at 12​12​3\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{2}3 in the U⁡(1)U(1) QSL, not present in the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL. By considering the long-range order at x=1x=1, which again differs between U⁡(1)U(1) and ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, we found that the x=0.33x=0.33 can be understood in terms of short-range ordered regions with glassy dynamics. This explains why previous neutron scattering measurements at 22\,K saw some structure (albeit far from diffraction limited), where the simplest expectation for a spin glass would be an isotropic ring of scattering Silverstein et al. 2014.

V.1 Limitations of our approximations

While both the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and U⁡(1)U(1) QSLs reproduce the full range of existing experimental data, ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} does slightly better in the sense that its predicted T∗T^{*} is closer to the experimental value (leading to a closer match to the χ⁡(T)\chi(T), S⁡(f,T)S(f,T), and qEAq_{\textrm{EA}} predictions). We do not read too much into this success, since some of our approximations are rather drastic and likely outweigh this small difference in predictions. Two approximations in particular could be removed with further work.

First, we treat the QSLs using mean field theory (self-consistent mean field theory for the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL; no self-consistency is required for U⁡(1)U(1)). A more accurate estimate of the interactions between witnesses could be obtained using exact diagonalisation or DMRG. This would naturally be at the expense of considering a reduced system size compared to ours (we considered up to 32×3232\times 32 unit cells). We note that there remains significant disagreement over the nature of the ground state of the KHAF, with some studies reporting the U⁡(1)U(1) QSL to be of lower energy, and others reporting ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}. Recent advances in machine learning approaches have led to a report that in fact the ground state is not a QSL at all, but is instead a spinon spin density wave. In order to obtain the witness couplings Ji​jJ_{ij}, these numerical methods would need to introduce a degree of three dimensionality, enhancing the issue.

Second, after integrating out the QSL, we then treat the witnesses as classical spins. This approximation is largely pragmatic as the system needs to be sufficiently large to get a sensible measure of spin glass behaviour. Being spin-1/2, the witnesses are maximally quantum, so the classical approximation is likely to present inaccuracies. Given the Ji​jJ_{ij} we have calculated, the relative sparseness of witnesses could make exact diagonalisation or DMRG plausible for estimating the resulting quantum witness behaviour. This would be highly desirable, since in principle the witnesses should inherit the long-range entanglement from the QSL. In this sense, the spin glass the witnesses form is really a new state of quantum matter: a long-range entangled spin glass. This could perhaps be detectable via measures such as the quantum Fisher information extracted from inelastic neutron scattering.

We further justify the approximation of the spins as classical Ising spins rather than Heisenberg spins. From a numerical perspective, the spin glass state was first explicitly demonstrated in an Ising spin system Binder and Stauffer 1976; Binder and Schröder 1976. Several early numerical studies with Heisenberg spin system had, initially, failed to produce a spin glass transition at finite temperature. Large scale computational study eventually produces phenomena consistent with spin glass state in isotropic Heisenberg spin models Banavar and Cieplak 1982; McMillan 1985; Olive et al. 1986. However, spin glass behaviour remains substantially more difficult to establish in these cases owing to finite-size effects Fernandez et al. 2009. Study of models with random anisotropic interaction are capable of producing spin glass behaviour more decisively, but these spin glass states were found to be in the same universality class as the Ising spin glass Matsubara et al. 1991; Baity-Jesi et al. 2014. This suggests that Heisenberg spin glass can be represented by an effective Ising model as in our case.

The Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interaction is likely to be significant for witnesses in Herbertsmithite Zorko et al. 2008; Heully-Alary et al. 2025. This could favour either an easy axis (Ising-like spins) along cc, or an easy plane (XY-like) perpendicular to it. A model properly incorporating this effect would be desirable.

V.2 Alternative Models

Both the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and U⁡(1)U(1) models give similar matches to existing experimental data. This begs the question as to whether other models, not involving QSLs, might also be compatible with current observations.

We can make certain clear statements on the possible forms of witness-witness interactions Ji​jJ_{ij} consistent with current experiments. (i) Neutron scattering at 22\,K shows that the nearest neighbour witness-witness interactions are antiferromagnetic and the dominant interaction Nilsen et al. 2013; Han et al. 2016. Spin glass formation at T∗=260T^{*}=260\,mK, evidenced by χ⁡(T)\chi(T), S⁡(f,T)S(f,T), and aging, shows that (ii) frustrating further neighbour interactions must exist; otherwise the lattice is trivially antiferromagnetic. The degree of frustration can be quantified by TCW/T∗=4.2T_{\textrm{CW}}/T^{*}=4.2. This adds a significant constraint on possible couplings according to the mean-field expression

TCW=S⁡(S+1)3​∑ini​Ji​0\displaystyle T_{\textrm{CW}}=\frac{S(S+1)}{3}\sum_{i}n_{i}J_{i0} (59)

where S=1/2S=1/2 and nin_{i} is the number of ithi^{\textrm{th}} nearest neighbours to witness site j=0j=0. (iii) In order for these further neighbour couplings not to destroy the match to neutron scattering, the interactions must decay at least as fast as 1/r21/r^{2} (if a 2D or semi-2D model such as ours is considered; otherwise 1/r31/r^{3} for a 3D interaction model). (iv) In addition, if near-neighbour magnetic exchange models are proposed, they must maintain sufficiently long-range exchange that the witnesses not present in the largest connected component do not lead to a divergent χ⁡(T)\chi(T) at low temperatures. Ref. Takahashi et al. 2026 measured down to 2020\,mK and saw no evidence for any upturn in χ⁡(T)\chi(T). (v) Any local exchange models must also not induce a significant AFM order parameter: even if this order parameter does not correspond to true long-range AFM order, its development at a specific temperature would lead to clear signatures in specific heat that are not seen Helton et al. 2007; de Vries et al. 2008; Kimchi et al. 2018; Murayama et al. 2022.

Together, constraints (i)-(v) significantly restrict any possible proposals for alternatives to QSL mediated interactions, even before any appeal is made to Occam’s razor to dismiss highly fine-tuned interactions. For example, we considered a model of magnon-mediated interactions based on the Kondo-Yamaji Green’s function decoupling Yu and Feng 2000; Bernhard et al. 2002; Legg and Braunecker 2019; this fell foul of (iii), subsequently failing to reproduce the observed neutron scattering pattern (Sec. II.4.3). We also conducted an extensive numerical search of local exchange models. First and second neighbours alone fall foul of (iv), giving a divergent χ⁡(T)\chi(T) at low temperatures. Still, density functional theory predictions for direct witness exchange pathways would be welcome. Various other models were considered and ruled out in Ref. Takahashi et al. 2026.

Ultimately, while restrictions (i)-(v) leave space for a range of possible witness-witness interactions, it remains non-trivial that the two successful QSL-based models we present meet all criteria. We suggest this lends considerable weight to the hypothesis that Herbertsmithite hosts a QSL within its kagome copper planes. We hope that our new prediction, that neutron scattering below 260260\,mK can distinguish the two candidate QSLs, will motivate further experiments.
